query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of boron to promote interface complexion engineering in eutectic high-entropy alloys will improve both strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility by enhancing the cohesion of the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that, in their conventional state, exhibit high strength but limited ductility due to microcrack initiation along weak interlamellar interfaces.
generation.intervention: Addition of a small boron content (e.g., on the order of 0.5–1 atomic %) during alloy fabrication to encourage boron segregation at the internal boundaries.
generation.conditions: The alloy must be processed under controlled solidification and subsequent thermo-mechanical treatments that ensure uniform distribution and effective segregation of boron, with evaluation under room-temperature tensile testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemically modified lamellar interfaces where boron segregation leads to the formation of enriched interfacial complexions or nanoscale precipitates that bolster the cohesion between phases.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to the internal lamellar boundaries, altering the interfacial energy and structure. This engineering of the interface enhances its strength and resistance to crack initiation, while simultaneously promoting more distributed plastic deformation (e.g., via dislocation activity) across the interface, thereby mitigating premature microcracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the boron-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and elongation to fracture at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys processed by conventional routes with unmodified, microcrack-prone lamellar interfaces that exhibit high strength but compromised ductility due to brittle failure along these boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only within a narrow boron concentration window (approximately 0.5–1 at.%), and under processing conditions that facilitate uniform boron segregation without forming deleterious brittle phases. Excess boron or inappropriate processing may instead impair mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of strength and ductility enhancement is uncertain and may be sensitive to precise boron concentration, segregation efficiency, and thermo-mechanical treatment parameters. The detailed evolution of the interfacial structure upon boron addition also remains to be fully clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples under identical processing conditions: one set with the optimized boron addition (around 0.5–1 at.%) and one control without boron. Characterize the interlamellar interfaces using high-resolution techniques (e.g., TEM with EDS) to verify boron segregation. Then perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure mechanical properties.
measurements: Interfacial chemical composition and morphology (via TEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and elongation compared to the control, or if interfacial characterization does not reveal evidence of boron-induced interface modification, then the hypothesis is falsified.
